title: The First 30 Days After an IPO: What Public Companies Should Prioritize
summary: Build a strong post-IPO foundation with guidance on financial reporting, internal controls, governance and investor communications.
body_markdown:
Completing[an initial public offering (IPO)](https://www.cbiz.com/services/advisory/financial-accounting-advisory/public-company-readiness-preparation) is a major milestone, but becoming a public company is only the beginning. In the first 30 days following an IPO, organizations face heightened expectations from regulators, investors and the market.


This early period can set the tone for investor confidence, regulatory compliance and the company’s ability to operate effectively in the public markets. Establishing discipline from the start is critical, particularly across four areas: financial reporting, internal controls, governance and communications.


## Establish Financial Reporting and Disclosure Discipline


The transition to public-company reporting brings new requirements, tighter timelines and increased scrutiny. Finance teams must quickly adjust to a more structured reporting environment while ensuring IPO-related accounting matters are appropriately addressed.


Clear roles and responsibilities are also essential. Finance, legal and investor relations need to work together to establish a reliable reporting process and maintain consistency across financial disclosures and other market-facing communications.


The goal during this initial period is not simply to meet the next filing deadline. It is to begin creating disciplined, repeatable processes that can support the company’s evolving reporting obligations.


## Move From SOX Readiness to Execution


For newly public companies, internal controls also become a heightened priority. While[Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) readiness](https://www.cbiz.com/services/advisory/risk-management-compliance/sarbanes-oxley-compliance-icfr) ideally begins before the IPO, the transition to the public markets shifts the emphasis toward executing and strengthening the company’s control environment.


Organizations should assess where gaps exist and identify areas that require additional documentation, remediation or oversight. Technology and cybersecurity considerations should also be incorporated into the broader internal control and risk management environment.


Addressing these areas early can help companies build a more sustainable approach to controls as requirements and expectations evolve.


## Put Governance Structures Into Action


An IPO also changes the expectations placed on a company’s governance structure. Boards and committees must move from preparation to active oversight, supported by appropriate policies, processes and reporting channels.


During the first month, organizations should focus on making sure governance structures are functioning as intended and aligned with the expectations that come with operating as a public company.


Getting this foundation right can help leadership manage risk, improve accountability and support more effective decision-making as the organization matures.


## Establish a Disciplined Communications Environment


Going public changes not only what an organization reports, but also how it communicates.


Public companies operate in a highly regulated disclosure environment, making coordination among leadership, investor relations, finance and legal especially important. Organizations need processes for reviewing external communications, managing material information and responding appropriately when events require disclosure.


A disciplined approach to communications can help a newly public company meet its regulatory responsibilities while also building consistency and credibility with investors and the broader market.


## What Comes After the First 30 Days?


The first month creates an important foundation, but public-company readiness doesn’t end there.


As organizations move beyond initial stabilization, the focus begins to shift. Processes must become repeatable. Internal controls and governance structures need to mature. Financial reporting must evolve to meet public-market expectations, while leadership builds a more established relationship with investors.


Over time, the objective is to move beyond meeting immediate compliance obligations and establish an operating model capable of supporting sustainable growth in the public markets.


## Build Your Post-IPO Roadmap


The first 30 days can set the trajectory, but they represent only one stage of the post-IPO journey.


Download[Post-IPO Roadmap: The First 180 Days for Public Companies](https://www2.cbiz.com/playbookforpostipogrowth) for practical guidance on navigating each phase after an IPO, from initial stabilization through building repeatable processes and ultimately creating a scalable public-company operating model.


Explore the financial reporting, internal control, governance, risk management and investor engagement priorities that can help your organization move beyond compliance and build a stronger foundation for long-term success.
